subject: Perfect fit but no standard error

messages.author: 8f8b5832b9ad8628
messages.subject: Perfect fit but no standard error
parts:
Dear all,

I have a very good-fitting model (e.g., CFI = 0.968), but the standard errors are all NA, can I use this model or some fix is needed? Thanks, Reza

m1 <- '
au_v=~ NA*audio_vocab_1+audio_vocab_2+audio_vocab_3+audio_vocab_4+audio_vocab_5+audio_vocab_6
ctst=~ NA*ctest_1+ctest_2+ctest_3+ctest_4+ctest_5+ctest_6
dict=~ NA*dictation_1+dictation_2+dictation_3+dictation_4+dictation_5+dictation_6
el_s=~ NA*elicited_speech_1+elicited_speech_2+elicited_speech_3+elicited_speech_4+elicited_speech_5+elicited_speech_6
tx_v=~ NA*text_vocab_1+text_vocab_2+text_vocab_3+text_vocab_4+text_vocab_5+text_vocab_6

DET = ~ NA*au_v+ctst+dict+el_s+tx_v
DET ~~ 1*DET

au_v ~~ 1*au_v
ctst ~~ 1*ctst
dict ~~ 1*dict
el_s ~~ 1*el_s
tx_v ~~ 1*tx_v '

w4 <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/izeh/m/master/w4.csv', stringsAsFactors = F) 
 
m1 <- sem(m1, data = w4, meanstructure = TRUE, missing = 'ML')

summary(m1, fit.measures=TRUE)

messages.author: e156e83d5c4b4d2f
messages.subject: Re: Perfect fit but no standard error
parts:
Thanks for submitting something easy to reproduce!

If you scroll up, you'll see the following error message: 

Warning message:
  In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
                      lavaan WARNING:
                      Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
                    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
                    identified.

As such, no, you cannot use the model and you need to fix something.  I'm not sure what's going on, but your parameter estimates look very unusual.  The amount of missingness (roughly 80%) in your last couple of variables might be the problem.

messages.subject: Re: Perfect fit but no standard error
parts:
My guess is that your issue is related to that. Those values are very different from the rest of your values and create a very unusual data pattern.  On the items that have those extreme values, it seems like 95% of your values tend to fall between -3 and +3, with the other 5% around -16 and +16.  

If so, this isn't a lavaan or sem issue but a data generation issue.

parts: I'm not sure, sorry!  I don't think so, because it isn't best practice to just delete outliers.  I would be careful about your next steps - make sure to only delete these values if they are true outliers (and not representative of something important that could change your theory or conclusions).
On Tue, May 5, 2020 at 9:47 PM Reza Norouzian <rnoro...@gmail.com> wrote:

Great point thank you! Is there an outlier elimination function in lavaan?

On Tue, May 5, 2020 at 11:42 PM Melissa Gordon Wolf <meliss...@ucsb.edu> wrote:
My guess is that your issue is related to that. Those values are very different from the rest of your values and create a very unusual data pattern.  On the items that have those extreme values, it seems like 95% of your values tend to fall between -3 and +3, with the other 5% around -16 and +16.  

If so, this isn't a lavaan or sem issue but a data generation issue.

On Tue, May 5, 2020 at 9:31 PM Reza Norouzian <rnoro...@gmail.com> wrote:
Yes, these are logit transformed.

Hi Reza,

Check out the descriptive statistics for your items.  Your min/max values for ctest_1 through elicited_speech_6 are -16/+18.  Is this intentional?

Melissa

Melissa,

But the last couple of variables are not included in the model!

On Tue, May 5, 2020 at 9:49 PM Melissa Gordon Wolf <meliss...@ucsb.edu> wrote:
Thanks for submitting something easy to reproduce!

If you scroll up, you'll see the following error message: 

Warning message:
  In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
                      lavaan WARNING:

                    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
                    identified.

As such, no, you cannot use the model and you need to fix something.  I'm not sure what's going on, but your parameter estimates look very unusual.  The amount of missingness (roughly 80%) in your last couple of variables might be the problem.

messages.subject: Re: Perfect fit but no standard error
parts:
Further to Melissa
the mis-match of scale can cause problems. see
Kim, J.-O., & Mueller, C. W. (1978). Factor analysis: Statistical methods and practical issues (Vol. 14). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage
Instead of deleting outliers, why not winsorize the scores so that you keep the cases but restrict the range for the extreme scores?
at least you should test the impact of deleting them vs. rescaling them
gavin

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: Perfect fit but no standard error
parts: If one set of variables falls in the range 1-6 (a Likert-style rating scale) and another variable falls in the range 100 to 1000, the variables have numeric scales of very different range. Not surprising this can cause real problems with calculating variance-covariance matrices. we found this in a 2008 study where we had rating scale values 1-6 and an achievement score M=700, SD=100. We had to reverse transform the test scores to IRT values with M=4.29, SD=1.61. The analysis engine was very happy regressing latent factors onto achievement once we did that.Of course whether logit values or transformed values the test scores had the same meaning, but SEM didn't like it with such a large mis-match of numeric range.
